"A total of 198 WHRDs were supported out of these where 129 new WHRDs from Zimbabwe and Malawi. The Areas in which WHRDs increased their L&A capacities are Political knowledge and leadership capacity; Economic strategies for resilience and stability; Use of storytelling, data analysis, power mapping, and research for advocacy; Awareness of issues like early marriage, water and transport challenges, violence, and threats to livelihoods from environmental changes. The types of Increased Lobby and Advocacy Capacities: Strengthened capacity (knowledge and skills) to advance women’s rights and gender equality through increased political knowledge, including awareness of repressive laws and structural violence. Enhanced leadership capacity to engage with municipal leaders and demand access to basic services. Strengthened economic strategies for resilience and stability, including control over resources and land. Skills in storytelling, data analysis, power mapping, in-depth interviews, triangulation of data sources, and using research for advocacy. Content of the Capacity Building Initiatives: The initiatives focused on increasing political knowledge, leadership capacity, economic strategies, and specific skills such as storytelling, data analysis, and power mapping. They also aimed at building awareness of issues affecting women and enhancing the ability to engage in advocacy and mobilization. Changes in Knowledge and Skills: The initiatives resulted in increased awareness of repressive laws, structural violence, and economic resilience. Skills in advocacy, data analysis, and mobilization were also enhanced.The types of lobby and advocacy capacities that were increased or developed among the Women Human Rights Defenders (WHRDs) include: Increased Political Knowledge: Understanding of repressive laws against women and structural violence, including historical and structural perspectives of exclusion and injustice. Leadership Capacity: The ability to engage municipal leaders and demand access to basic services, as well as taking up leadership positions in both formal and informal settings. This includes tapping into existing leadership capacities for community and political engagement. Economic Strategies: Development and strengthening of strategies for economic resilience and stability, including control over resources and land, and the establishment of community women’s savings groups (“mukando”). Awareness Raising: Increased community awareness about issues such as the negative impacts of infrastructure projects (e.g., dam construction) on communities and the importance of environmental conservation. Storytelling: Utilizing personal and community stories as a tool for advocacy and to influence debates and discussions around women’s rights and gender equality. Data Analysis: The ability to analyze data in a way that supports advocacy efforts, including understanding the implications of data on women’s rights and gender equality. Power Mapping: Identifying key stakeholders and understanding the dynamics of power relations within a given context to effectively target advocacy efforts. In-depth Interviews: Conducting thorough interviews to gather qualitative data and insights that can inform advocacy strategies and actions. Triangulation of Data Sources: Using multiple sources of data to validate findings and strengthen the evidence base for advocacy campaigns. Using Research for Advocacy: Applying research findings to advocate for policy changes, raise awareness, and mobilize support for women’s rights issues. Engagement in Political Processes: Participating in election agenda-setting processes, drafting policy briefs, and using collectively agreed demands to engage with authorities. Mobilization and Building Power in the Community: Applying the power analysis framework to mobilize community members and build collective power for social change. Articulating Demands to Government Officials: Enhancing skills to better communicate and negotiate with government representatives to address women’s needs and rights. These capacities encompass a broad range of skills and knowledge areas that enable WHRDs to effectively advocate for women’s rights and gender equality, engage in political processes, and mobilize communities for social change."

JASS created 5 new alliances in Zimbabwe in 2024 in an effort to keep feminist movements coming together to create collective agendas and analyse power together in order to be collectively stronger. Allies were able to strengthen their analysis to provide the most established movement building FPE tool with their communities. Allies who had previously engaged with the power analysis tool were able to see how JASS has updated it after years of research and those who have never used the power analysis tool, were able to strengthen their ability to use this tool with their communities for the first time as a method of facilitating movement building.

"JASS influenced debate on Pan-Africanism and was able to surface the intersectionality of oppression that women face and find synergies across different Black women's struggles/ movements. Through this engagement JASS influenced AGS and other donors present to support Black feminist movements, particularly channeling flexible resources - to be able to rapidly respond to safety and basic needs of women activists.The theme of the meeting was Black/African Feminism - What is it, and how does it differ from other feminisms? The objective of the meeting was to reflect on Black/African Feminism and our work.the meeting was organized by AGSNew alliances x 6quotes- What struck me was my own meaning of feminism which I said that feminist is all about equality . which put us in the forefront of all these struggles that we fight for. as human beings we are not equal so we want to make sure that things are equal between us. I have learn that through partnership with AGS there are more connections or similarities on work that we do as organization's for example issues of climate crisis and learning how crisis looks like we are all doing this in a different way hence the need for the partnership to work as a collective. Rebuilding our food system, building our voice and agency of women to challenge power we are all doing this in different ways and there is need to stop organizing in silosThe surveillance of women, risk and safety nets, issues of legal support for women who speak out about their struggles because they are put on the spotlight need to be taken seriously and put measures on it.In preparation for the meeting at the embassy, WHRDs were provided with the skills to:1. Use stories of change for advocacy2. Use their skills to advocate for additional support from the Dutch government (power holder)As a result, the ambassador said she would look at different ways that her team and her could support the WHRDs. Through using storytelling/ change stories that demonstrate women's lived experiences they were able to influence debate on feminist MEL and sharing collaborative ways of collecting and analysing data such as the FPAR process. New alliances were also formed during the meeting as different movement groups that were funded through the ""Strengthening Civil Society"" stream met at the embassy"

The Anti-retroviral treatment manual is a resource that provides women with the knowledge and skills to advocate for their rights to access quality health care services. It provides a written record in their local language so they can understand what rights they have for HIV treatment. In combination with JASS' other work, women now have both the knowledge and skills to demand ongoing and rights-based treatment for HIV, reducing their sickness and stigmatisation.
